g.text: Checkpoints and state stores — the pair, and what it costs to write
full 14 vs incremental 8 entry-uploads at k=3 (43% less) · replay 0/2/4/8 at k=1/3/5/9
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · 7 state entries · total 45
WHAT IS WRITTEN AT A CHECKPOINT TAKEN AFTER EVENT 4
two things, written together or the recovery is wrong
the state
4 entries, holding 23 in total
the source offset
4 — the position the state corresponds to
why BOTH
state without the offset replays events already counted
the damage if the offset is stale
22 double-counted from 4 re-applied events
The offset is not bookkeeping — it is half the checkpoint. A snapshot that does not say WHERE it was taken cannot be resumed from.
And the two must be committed atomically: state-then-crash double counts, offset-then-crash loses data.
Step 1/4 — a checkpoint is a snapshot plus a stream position
A checkpoint is a pair, and the pairing is the point. The state says what the aggregation holds; the offset says which prefix of the stream it
holds. Commit them non-atomically and ch05's scenario follows exactly: state saved but offset stale re-applies 4 events worth 22.
Checkpoints and state stores — the pair, and what it costs to write
full 14 vs incremental 8 entry-uploads at k=3 (43% less) · replay 0/2/4/8 at k=1/3/5/9
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · 7 state entries · total 45
WHY AN EMBEDDED STORE RATHER THAN A HASH MAP
a storage decision, with no effect on semantics
this stream's state
7 entries — fits in memory trivially
what makes it not fit
the entry count scales with keys x OPEN windows, both unbounded
an embedded store (e.g. RocksDB)
hot entries in memory, the rest on local disk
what it does NOT change
the entries, their values, or when they can be collected
The store is an implementation of the same 7-entry map. Nothing about windowing, triggers or watermarks changes because it spilled to disk.
What DOES change is the checkpoint cost, because now a snapshot means reading those bytes back off disk and uploading them.
Step 2/4 — state stores hold the bytes when it does not fit in memory
Worth separating cleanly: the state store is about where bytes live, and it changes nothing semantic. The 7 entries, their values and their
collection times are identical whether they sit in a hash map or in RocksDB. The consequence that does matter is in the note — once state is on
disk, checkpointing it becomes an I/O cost worth measuring.
Checkpoints and state stores — the pair, and what it costs to write
full 14 vs incremental 8 entry-uploads at k=3 (43% less) · replay 0/2/4/8 at k=1/3/5/9
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · 7 state entries · total 45
FULL VS INCREMENTAL, CHECKPOINTING EVERY 3 EVENTS
checkpoints at events 2, 5, 8 — what each one has to upload
checkpoint at event 2
FULL: 2 entries (all of the state)
INCREMENTAL: 2 entries (changed since)
checkpoint at event 5
FULL: 5 entries (all of the state)
INCREMENTAL: 3 entries (changed since)
checkpoint at event 8
FULL: 7 entries (all of the state)
INCREMENTAL: 3 entries (changed since)
Across the run: 14 entry-uploads full against 8 incremental — a 43% saving on 9 events.
And the gap WIDENS, because full scales with total state while incremental scales with churn. On a large, mostly-idle state the difference is
uploading 10 GB or 10 KB.
Step 3/4 — incremental checkpoints upload the churn, not the state
The numbers make the asymmetry visible: full uploads grow every checkpoint (2, 5, 7) while incremental ones track churn (2, 3, 3). 14 against 8
here, and the ratio keeps improving as state grows relative to how fast it changes.
Checkpoints and state stores — the pair, and what it costs to write
full 14 vs incremental 8 entry-uploads at k=3 (43% less) · replay 0/2/4/8 at k=1/3/5/9
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · 7 state entries · total 45
CHECKPOINT EVERY k EVENTS — I/O AGAINST RECOVERY
how many checkpoints, how much is uploaded, and the worst-case replay
9 checkpoints
9 entry-uploads (incremental)
worst-case replay: 0 events
3 checkpoints
8 entry-uploads (incremental)
worst-case replay: 2 events
1 checkpoint
4 entry-uploads (incremental)
worst-case replay: 4 events
1 checkpoint
7 entry-uploads (incremental)
worst-case replay: 8 events
k = 1 replays 0 events and uploads 9 times; k = 9 replays 8 and uploads 7.
Both ends are correct. The choice is a failure-budget question: how long may recovery take, and how much steady-state I/O is affordable?
Step 4/4 — and the frequency is a trade with no free point
Four frequencies, and the trade is monotone in both directions — no setting is free. Checkpoint every event and recovery replays 0 but you pay 9
uploads; checkpoint once and you pay 7 upload and replay 8 events. The number to start from is the recovery time you can tolerate, not the I/O you
would prefer.
